sysd-reliab-075.title: Rate limiting: capping how often an operation may run
sysd-reliab-075.text:
Left unwatched, auto-scaling can lead to exponential bills. One of the jobs of rate limiting is to put a virtual cap on it. Rate limiting prevents the frequency of an operation from exceeding a defined limit, and large-scale systems use it as a defensive mechanism that lets shared resources stay available.

For an API, the limit caps how many requests can reach it in a given period, which guards against unintended or malicious overuse. It avoids the resource starvation that denial-of-service attacks cause, limits web scraping and can mitigate some other common attacks; see {{ref:sysd-blocks-180}}. Data centers use it to share resources among tenants and applications according to the terms of their service agreements, covered in {{ref:sysd-reliab-100}}.

In practice, a server checks the user session or IP address against a session cache, often a central in-memory key-value store such as Redis or Aerospike. An HTTP server can answer too many requests with status 429. Over the limit, a server or device offloads new requests without responding, or queues them. At peak times the request rate can exceed the queue capacity, and then requests are thrown away.

Placement matters. A hardware appliance limiting by IP address on layer 4 risks blocking a whole network of users behind one NAT address. For dynamic content, the limiting logic should be built into the application.

sysd-reliab-082.title: Fault tolerance: keeping going while parts are broken
sysd-reliab-082.text:
A system that fails only rarely is not necessarily fault tolerant. If it stops operating completely when a fault does occur, it is fault resistant instead. Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to contain the propagation of faults and keep operating without failure while some components are faulty.

A fault may show up as an error, such as a bad data value or a missing message, that leaves the system in an incorrect state. A fault-tolerant system masks the error. Strictly, that means no degradation or downtime and users unaware of any issue. A system that suffers some interruption or a decline in performance is called resilient instead; see {{ref:sysd-reliab-084}}.

It requires no single point of failure. It also requires dedicated failure detection to isolate the faulty component, containment so a failure does not propagate, and reversion modes that abandon recent changes. Such systems rest on redundancy and are judged by availability: five nines statistically means 99.999%. Redundancy costs money and design time, so making every component fault tolerant is normally not an option.

sysd-reliab-083.title: Fault tolerance techniques: replicas, standbys and spare parts
sysd-reliab-083.text:
Fault tolerance has no single trick. It has a toolbox, and every tool works the same way: a spare or independent component is ready, so a failure does not stop the service.

Replication runs multiple identical instances in parallel, sends requests to all of them and picks the correct result by quorum. ByteByteGo describes it more broadly, as multiple copies of data or services across nodes or locations. Redundancy also provides multiple identical instances, but it switches to a remaining one when a failure occurs, which is failover. Diversity goes a step further. It provides multiple different implementations of the same specification and uses them like replicas, to cope with errors in one specific implementation.

Load balancing distributes incoming traffic across servers so no single server becomes a point of failure, and failover mechanisms switch to a standby when the primary fails. Continuous watching of system health and performance, with alerts for anomalies or failures, is one of the six principles ByteByteGo lists. The others are replication, redundancy, load balancing, failover and a fallback to reduced service, described in {{ref:sysd-reliab-084}}. The watching itself is the subject of {{ref:sysd-reliab-201}}.

Storage has its own example: every RAID level except RAID 0 is a fault-tolerant storage device that uses data redundancy. One more technique to avoid catastrophic failures in distributed systems is described in {{ref:sysd-reliab-067}}.

sysd-reliab-168.title: Cascading failure: when one outage causes the next
sysd-reliab-168.text:
Lose one cluster, and the survivor can end up serving less than it did before. Suppose cluster B fails and cluster A's load rises from 1,000 to 1,200 QPS. A's frontends run out of resources, and successful requests fall below 1,000 QPS. This is a cascading failure. In a system of interconnected parts, the failure of one or a few parts causes other parts to fail, and the damage grows progressively through positive feedback.

The cause is compensation. When one part fails, the others must pick up its work, and that overloads them so they fail too. Once a couple of servers crash, the rest take more load and crash in turn, until all servers crash-loop. Restarted servers are bombarded with requests and fail almost immediately, so recovery is hard. A cache stampede is one kind of cascade.

Local overload can spread to other failure domains, even globally, in only a couple of minutes, because load balancers and schedulers act quickly. Watching the system in real time and judiciously disconnecting parts can help stop a cascade.

sysd-reliab-176.title: Deadline propagation: passing the remaining time down the call tree
sysd-reliab-176.text:
Servers that waste resources on requests already past the client's deadline are a common theme in cascading outages. An RPC deadline says how long a request may wait before the caller gives up, so it limits how long a backend can consume a frontend's resources. With no deadline, or an extremely high one, long-gone problems keep consuming server resources. At a 100-second deadline, 5% of requests hitting it would need 5,000 threads on a 1,000-thread frontend.

Deadline propagation passes the remaining time down the whole call tree. A deadline is set high in the stack, and every RPC in the tree shares the same absolute deadline. A 30-second deadline with 7 seconds spent leaves 23 seconds for the next call, then 19. Without propagation, B might use a hardcoded 20-second deadline after A gave it only 10 seconds. Then C processes a request believing it has 15 seconds, although the deadline has passed. A server should check the remaining deadline before each stage instead of doing work nobody will credit.

sysd-reliab-178.title: Resource exhaustion: when a server runs out of room
sysd-reliab-178.text:
Run short of CPU, and soon the server is short of everything else. Resource exhaustion is a server running out of CPU, memory, threads or file descriptors under load, and it can start a cascading failure. A file descriptor is the handle a process uses for an open file or network connection.

With too little CPU, all requests slow down, so more are in flight at once. They use more memory, threads, file descriptors and backend resources, and queues saturate. Late responses may miss client deadlines, so the work is wasted and clients retry, adding overload. In Java, memory pressure raises garbage collection, the runtime's cleanup of unused memory, and that raises CPU use, so less CPU slows requests further. This is the so-called GC death spiral. Thread starvation or exhausted file descriptors can make health checks fail, and watchdogs may then kill the server.

These scenarios feed one another, so an overloaded service shows secondary symptoms that look like the root cause. The load balancer then shifts the problem to other servers, and a cascade can follow.

sysd-reliab-170.title: Load shedding: refusing some work to finish the rest
sysd-reliab-170.text:
Past its breaking point, a service does better to let some errors through than to try to serve every request. Load shedding drops some proportion of traffic as a server approaches overload, so the server keeps doing useful work instead of failing. The goal is to keep it from running out of RAM, failing health checks or serving with extremely high latency.

A straightforward way is per-task throttling based on CPU, memory or queue length. One effective approach returns HTTP 503 to any request when more than a given number of client requests are in flight. Shedding can be indiscriminate, dropping all traffic above X requests per second. It can also be selective, dropping low-priority work such as background synchronization while still serving interactive user sessions. Switching the queue from first-in first-out to last-in first-out, or using the CoDel algorithm, removes requests unlikely to be worth processing.

The code path you never use often does not work. So regularly run a small subset of servers near overload to exercise it.

sysd-reliab-171.title: Client-side throttling: slowing down before the backend says no
sysd-reliab-171.text:
Rejecting a request still costs resources. For cheap work, such as a lookup in RAM, it costs almost as much as serving it. A backend can be overloaded while most of its CPU goes to rejecting. Client-side throttling moves the refusal to the caller. A client that sees many recent requests rejected caps its own outgoing traffic, and requests above the cap fail locally.

In adaptive throttling, each client task keeps, for the last two minutes, the requests attempted by the application and the requests accepted by the backend. Clients keep sending until requests reach K times accepts. After that, they reject new requests locally, with a probability that rises as the request rate grows relative to the accepted rate.

Self-regulating at requests = 1.1 * accepts means the backend rejects only one request per 10 accepted. The SRE book prefers a 2x multiplier, which wastes some resources but spreads backend state faster. The decision is purely local, so it adds no dependencies or latency, but it may not work well for clients that send requests only sporadically.

sysd-reliab-169.title: Bandwidth throttling: limiting how fast data moves
sysd-reliab-169.text: Client requests peak, and responses can be huge. Together they can exceed the capacity of parts of the network, causing congestion, request failures and, in the worst case, server crashes. Bandwidth throttling is the limiting of the rate of data transfer to or from a network node or device, such as a computer or mobile phone. A server throttles how fast it receives or sends data so it does not overload its processing capacity or saturate network bandwidth. Limiting at the sender is more efficient, because no packets are lost. Unlike rate limiting, which works on requests, it limits data, so the two should be paired.

sysd-reliab-088.title: Token bucket: letting bursts through at a steady average
sysd-reliab-088.text:
Picture a bucket that gets a token every 1/r seconds and holds at most b of them. A token arriving at a full bucket is discarded. That is the token bucket, an algorithm that checks whether traffic conforms to limits on bandwidth and burstiness.

A packet of n bytes conforms if at least n tokens are in the bucket. Then n tokens are removed and the packet is sent. Otherwise no tokens are removed and the packet is non-conformant. Non-conformant packets can be queued until enough tokens accumulate, or sent marked and possibly dropped later. A conforming flow can average up to the token rate, with burstiness set by the depth of the bucket.

In API rate limiting, each request must take a token. A request is refused when none is available, so the requester has to try again later as the bucket refreshes. The same bucket can delay packets until they conform or drop nonconforming ones, the two jobs of {{ref:sysd-reliab-087}}.

sysd-reliab-086.title: Leaky bucket: a constant leak and an overflow
sysd-reliab-086.text:
Pour water into a bucket with a constant leak, and it overflows if the water arrives faster than it leaks, or all at once beyond the bucket's capacity. The leaky bucket is an algorithm built on that analogy. It checks whether discrete events conform to limits on average and peak rates, and it can delay the actions tied to them until they conform.

It comes in two forms. As a meter, a counter goes up as each packet or event arrives and down at a fixed rate. The event conforms if the counter stays below a limit, meaning the bucket does not overflow. As a queue, it is a finite FIFO buffer serviced at a fixed rate. An arrival is appended if there is room and discarded otherwise. The queue version is a special case of the meter version, with gaps in its output when the queue empties.

For API rate limiting, the queue version appends each request to a queue and processes the first item at a regular interval. Additional requests are discarded when the queue is full.

sysd-reliab-078.title: Resilience patterns: keeping a small error small
sysd-reliab-078.text:
The largest incidents are usually caused by something very small. A minor error starts a snowball effect that keeps building up, and suddenly everything is down. Resilience patterns are design patterns that limit the damage failures do, so a small error does not snowball into an outage.

The usual set is rate limiting, load shedding, back pressure, let it crash and one more pattern, described in {{ref:sysd-reliab-067}}. That pattern wraps a protected call and trips once failures reach a threshold. Further calls then return an error without the call being made. Rate limiting keeps shared resources available, but it ignores overall service health, so it may not stop a failure already begun. Load shedding drops some traffic as a server approaches overload. Back pressure limits the queue size. Once the queue fills, clients get a server-busy or HTTP 503 status and try again later.

Retries must be bounded or they amplify an overload. These patterns are usually not used alone, so know why each is needed, how it works and its limits.

sysd-reliab-085.title: Fail fast or fail safe: choosing how a system breaks
sysd-reliab-085.text: Some designs choose how they break. A fail-fast component reports at the first point of failure rather than after downstream components fail. That allows easier diagnosis and may prevent improper operation in a broken state. A fail-safe design fails in a way that protects people, property or data from injury, damage, intrusion or disclosure. It may keep working at a reduced level or fail completely. A program can fail safe by exiting gracefully instead of crashing in an uncontrolled way, which prevents data corruption after an error. To achieve fault tolerance, Singh's guide advises microservices to fail fast with the pattern described in {{ref:sysd-reliab-067}}.

sysd-reliab-084.title: Graceful degradation: doing less instead of stopping
sysd-reliab-084.text: A video stream that drops to a lower resolution when bandwidth runs short has not failed. It has degraded. A system designed for graceful degradation, also called failing soft, keeps running at reduced functionality or performance after a component fails instead of failing completely. A building that runs its lighting at reduced levels after a grid failure does the same. So does progressive enhancement: web pages are available in a basic functional format for limited browsers and in an enhanced version for capable ones. In resilience terms, the system adapts to the error and maintains service while accepting some impact on performance.

sysd-reliab-181.title: Recovering from a cascading failure
sysd-reliab-181.text:
Once a cascade is under way, some fixes make it worse. Recovery means identifying the cascade, then adding capacity, reducing load, restarting wedged servers or degrading service until the system stabilizes.

If you have idle resources, adding tasks is the most expedient recovery, though in a death spiral it may not be enough. Health checking can itself make a service unhealthy, so disabling it temporarily can help. Dropping load is a big hammer. If a service healthy at 10,000 QPS fails at 11,000, dropping to 9,000 will not stop the crashes. With 10% of servers healthy, it would need about 1,000 QPS.

If the whole service is crash-looping, be aggressive and let through perhaps 1% of traffic. Then ramp up gradually so caches warm up. Fix the root cause first, or the cascade returns with the traffic. Restart wedged servers only after finding the source of the failure, and go slowly, since a cold cache could make restarts amplify it. Serving degraded results and turning off important but not critical load, such as index updates, also cut load.

sysd-reliab-076.title: Rate limiting algorithms: five ways to count requests
sysd-reliab-076.text:
Five algorithms do most of the work in rate limiting, and each has its own advantages and disadvantages. They are the leaky bucket, the token bucket, the fixed window, the sliding log and the sliding window.

Leaky bucket appends each request to a queue that is processed first-in, first-out at a regular interval. When the queue is full, additional requests are discarded. Token bucket requires each request to take a token from a bucket. With no token available, the request is refused and the requester must try again later, and the bucket refreshes after a time period.

Fixed window tracks a counter for a window of n seconds, increments it on each request and discards the request when the counter exceeds a threshold. Sliding log keeps a time-stamped log for each request in a time-sorted hash set or table and discards logs whose timestamps are beyond a threshold. For a new request, it sums the logs to find the request rate and holds the request if it would exceed the threshold rate.

Sliding window is a hybrid. It keeps fixed window's low processing cost and sliding log's better boundary behavior, adding a weighted value of the previous window's rate to smooth traffic bursts.

sysd-reliab-077.title: Rate limiting across a cluster of servers
sysd-reliab-077.text:
A consumer who sends requests to different nodes can exceed a limit that each node enforces separately. A cluster may need a global rate limit, and if each node tracks its own, more nodes make that overrun likelier. Rate limiting across a cluster is hard because of inconsistent per-node counters and race conditions on shared counters.

Sticky sessions in the load balancer send each consumer to exactly one node, but they cause a lack of fault tolerance and scaling problems. A centralized data store such as Redis is another approach, but it increases latency and causes race conditions. In a naive get-then-set counter, the server reads the count, increments it and writes it back. Extra requests slip in during that cycle and store stale lower values, so a consumer can bypass the limit.

A distributed lock around the counter key prevents that race, but the lock becomes a significant bottleneck and does not scale well. A set-then-get approach lets counters be incremented and checked quickly without atomic operations getting in the way.

sysd-reliab-173.title: Measuring capacity beyond queries per second
sysd-reliab-173.text: Queries per second sounds like a measure of capacity, but it is often a poor one. Different queries need vastly different resources, depending on factors such as the client code issuing them or the time of day. The ratios can change, sometimes drastically after a software release. A better solution is to measure capacity directly in resources, for example 500 CPU cores and 1 TB of memory reserved for a service in a datacenter. The cost of a request is then a normalized measure of CPU time, and CPU consumption usually works as the provisioning signal.

sysd-reliab-172.title: Per-customer quotas: errors only for the misbehaving
sysd-reliab-172.text: When a shared backend is overloaded, only the misbehaving customers should see errors. Global overload occurs quite frequently, especially for internal services with many clients, and per-customer quotas cap the resources each customer may use so that other customers remain unaffected. Owners provision capacity from negotiated usage and set a quota for each customer. One client of a 10,000-CPU backend might get up to 4,000 CPU seconds per second. Quotas may sum above capacity, since customers rarely all peak together. Global usage is aggregated in real time from all backend tasks, and effective limits are pushed to individual tasks.

sysd-reliab-174.title: Request criticality: rejecting the least important first
sysd-reliab-174.text: Search suggestions shown while typing are highly sheddable, yet their latency requirements are stringent. So criticality is independent of latency needs. Criticality tags each request with how important it is, so an overloaded backend rejects the least critical traffic first. A request has one of four values. CRITICAL_PLUS marks the most critical, a default covers production jobs, and SHEDDABLE_PLUS is the batch default, where partial unavailability is expected. A lowest tier sits below. A task rejects requests of one criticality only once it is rejecting all lower ones. The RPC system propagates criticality, so requests issued while serving request A inherit it.

openers.reliab: The largest incidents are usually caused by something very small. A minor error starts a snowball effect that keeps building, and suddenly everything is down. This part of the course is about the designs that stop the snowball. It starts with the failure that grows on its own, where the loss of one or a few parts overloads the rest and feeds itself through positive feedback. Then come the defenses: spare components that keep a service running while some parts are faulty, limits on how much traffic a server accepts, and the algorithms that count it.
openers.resilience-circuit-breakers-rate-limitin: Rate limiting prevents the frequency of an operation from exceeding a defined limit, and it is the first of the defenses in this chapter. Around it sit the ways a system keeps operating while some components are faulty, and the ways one failure turns into many. Next come the controls that stop the spread: a server that drops some traffic as it approaches overload, a deadline that tells the caller when to give up, and a client that slows itself before the backend must refuse it. The chapter then turns to the bucket algorithms that count traffic and to retries, and it ends with two protections around them: {{ref:sysd-reliab-067}} and {{ref:sysd-reliab-071}}.
